prompt: On the recording machine, `ls -l /dev/kvm` answered `No such file or directory`. What could that machine not do?
hint: An emulator is itself a virtual machine.

choices.text: Start an Android emulator
choices.why: Right: on Linux an emulator needs the processor's virtualisation, reached through `/dev/kvm`.

choices.text: Build an APK with `./gradlew assembleDebug`
choices.why: Building runs on the JVM and needs no virtualisation; lesson 1 built one on that very machine.

choices.text: Run Compose tests under Robolectric and save screenshots
choices.why: Robolectric runs inside an ordinary JVM test, which is exactly why the course uses it.

choices.text: Download the SDK from Google
choices.why: The download worked; `/dev/kvm` has nothing to do with the network.

prompt: A Roborazzi screenshot of a screen is in this course. What does it NOT tell you about the app?
hint: It is the drawing, not the device.

choices.text: Which text and colours the composable drew
choices.why: That is exactly what it shows: the PNG is what the composable drew.

choices.text: How quickly the app starts on a cheap phone
choices.why: Right: the test runs on your computer's JVM, so start-up time on a device is outside what it measures.

choices.text: What changed on screen after a test clicked a button
choices.why: A test can click and then capture, so the change is visible.

choices.text: Where the layout put each element
choices.why: Layout is computed on the JVM as on a phone, and the PNG shows it.

prompt: Why does section 03 rename the unpacked `cmdline-tools` folder to `cmdline-tools/latest`?
hint: Section 04 shows what happens without it.

choices.text: So that a later version can be unpacked beside it
choices.why: Several versions can live side by side, but that is not why the rename is required: the tools refuse to run without it.

choices.text: Because `PATH` cannot contain a directory called `cmdline-tools`
choices.why: `PATH` takes any directory name; the problem is the tools' own expectation.

choices.text: The tools locate the SDK from their own position, two levels up
choices.why: Right: without it they print `Could not determine SDK root`.

choices.text: Android Studio refuses an SDK whose tools are not called `latest`
choices.why: The refusal came from the command-line tools themselves; Studio was never run here.

prompt: A tutorial from 2024 says `sdkmanager "platforms;android-34"`. What is the same request to the Android CLI?
hint: One character changes.

choices.text: `android sdk install platforms/android-34`
choices.why: Right: the CLI writes package paths with a slash where `sdkmanager` used a semicolon.

choices.text: `android install platforms;android-34`
choices.why: `android install` installs an APK on a device; SDK packages go through `android sdk install`.

choices.text: `android sdk install --api 34`
choices.why: There is no `--api` option; the package is named in full.

choices.text: Nothing: `sdkmanager` refuses to run at all now
choices.why: It still runs: it prints a deprecation warning and hands the work to the CLI.

prompt: Which part of this setup is the one the course says it cannot pin to a version?
hint: It downloads itself the first time it runs.

choices.text: The platform package `platforms/android-37.0`
choices.why: A platform is named by its exact version, so it is pinned.

choices.text: The command-line tools zip
choices.why: The zip's name carries its build number, 16111833, which pins it.

choices.text: The Android CLI that the launcher fetches
choices.why: Right: the launcher always downloads the latest CLI; this course was recorded with 1.1.16717390.

choices.text: Gradle, because the wrapper picks the newest release
choices.why: The wrapper names an exact Gradle, 9.8.2, in `distributionUrl`.

prompt: Match each SDK package to what it gives the project.
hint: Section 03 installs three and names each.

The tools that package and sign an app, `aapt2` among them
`adb`, which talks to a phone or an emulator

prompt: `ls -lh` showed the size of the command-line tools zip. How many megabytes?
hint: The column before the date.

prompt: `android --version` prints `command not found` and `echo $?` prints 127, yet `ls` finds the file. What is wrong?
hint: 127 is the shell's number.

choices.text: The zip was damaged in the download
choices.why: A damaged file would be found and then fail; here the shell never found it.

choices.text: This terminal has not read the new lines in `~/.bashrc`
choices.why: Right: a terminal reads `~/.bashrc` when it starts. Open a new one, or `source ~/.bashrc`.

choices.text: `ANDROID_HOME` points at the wrong directory
choices.why: The shell finds commands through `PATH`, not `ANDROID_HOME`; the Gradle plugin is what reads the second.

choices.text: The CLI needs a licence to be accepted first
choices.why: The licence is shown on the first run, which never happened: the program was not found.

prompt: A build stops with `SDK location not found` on a machine where `android sdk list` works. Which fix does section 04 recommend?
hint: One of the two places is a file with a path of your computer in it.

choices.text: Commit a `local.properties` with `sdk.dir` to the project's repository
choices.why: It would work for you and name a path that does not exist on anybody else's machine; it never goes into version control.

choices.text: Reinstall the platform package with `--force`
choices.why: The SDK is installed and fine; the build simply does not know where it is.

choices.text: Open a terminal that has `ANDROID_HOME` set, from `~/.bashrc`
choices.why: Right: the variable is the first place the plugin looks, and it names no path inside the project.

choices.text: Add `ANDROID_HOME` to `gradle.properties`
choices.why: The plugin reads an environment variable or `sdk.dir`; a Gradle property of that name is not one of its two places.

prompt: What exit status does the shell give a command it cannot find?
hint: `echo $?` printed it in section 04.

prompt: `gradle/libs.versions.toml` lists Room, Retrofit and Hilt. What does the first build of lesson 1 download for them?
hint: Listing is not asking.

choices.text: Nothing: no module's build file asks for them yet
choices.why: Right: the catalogue names versions, and Gradle fetches a library only when a module declares it.

choices.text: All three, so that later lessons build offline
choices.why: A catalogue entry downloads nothing; lessons 12 to 15 fetch them when their build files ask.

choices.text: Only their version metadata, to check the numbers exist
choices.why: Gradle does not check unused catalogue entries against a repository.

choices.text: Their Gradle plugins, because the root build file loads them
choices.why: This is half right about plugins, which `apply false` does load, and wrong about the libraries the question asks about.

prompt: Which value in `app/build.gradle.kts` can never change once the app is published on Google Play?
hint: It is the app's identity on a phone.

choices.text: `versionName`
choices.why: It is the text users see, and it changes with every release.

choices.text: `namespace`
choices.why: It names the package of the generated `R` class and can be refactored; the store never sees it.

choices.text: `applicationId`
choices.why: Right: a different id is a different app to the phone and to the store.

choices.text: `compileSdk`
choices.why: It changes whenever you move to a newer API; it changes nothing on a phone.

prompt: Why does `robolectric.properties` say `sdk=35` when the app's `targetSdk` is 36?
hint: Read the error the section quotes.

choices.text: Robolectric 4.17 could not start Android 36 on this JDK
choices.why: Right: every test failed at start-up with `Failed to interact with raw FileDescriptor internals`.

choices.text: Tests have to run one version below the target, as a rule
choices.why: There is no such rule; the course would use 36 if Robolectric started it.

choices.text: 35 is the `minSdk`, the oldest phone the app supports
choices.why: `minSdk` is 26 in this project.

choices.text: The platform package installed in section 03 is 35
choices.why: Section 03 installed `platforms/android-37.0`; Robolectric downloads its own Android.

prompt: Inside the project you build with `./___ assembleDebug`, the script that runs the Gradle the project names.
hint: Section 05 wrote it with `gradle wrapper`.

prompt: Put the files in the order Gradle needs them to understand the project, starting from what it reads first.
hint: The settings say which modules exist.

prompt: The second `assembleDebug`, with nothing changed, finished in seconds. Why?
hint: Count the tasks that ran.

choices.text: Gradle skipped every task whose inputs had not changed
choices.why: Right: none of the 36 tasks ran again.

choices.text: The second build skipped the compile and only packaged
choices.why: Packaging is also a task with inputs, and it was skipped too.

choices.text: The debug build is incremental and the release build is not
choices.why: Both use the same up-to-date checks; the difference between them is R8 and signing.

choices.text: The Gradle daemon kept the APK in memory
choices.why: The APK is on disk, and the speed comes from tasks that did not run.

prompt: Match each of the three SDK numbers to the question it answers.
hint: Only one of them changes behaviour on a phone.

pairs.right: Which Android's API does the compiler know?
What is the oldest Android allowed to install the app?
Whose rules has the app opted into?

right_distractors: Which Android does Robolectric pretend to be?

prompt: An app raises `targetSdk` from 32 to 33 and changes no code. What does a user on Android 13 notice?
hint: From 33, a notification needs to be asked for.

choices.text: Nothing, because only `compileSdk` affects devices
choices.why: It is the other way round: `compileSdk` changes nothing on a phone and `targetSdk` opts into new rules.

choices.text: The app's notifications stop appearing until it asks for the permission
choices.why: Right: targeting 33 opts into the rule that a notification needs `POST_NOTIFICATIONS`, which lesson 19 asks for.

choices.text: The app can no longer be installed on Android 12
choices.why: That is `minSdk`'s job, and it did not change.

choices.text: The build fails until the code calls the Android 13 API
choices.why: Nothing requires the code to call a newer API; the build is unaffected.

prompt: The merged manifest has a permission you never wrote. Where did it most likely come from?
hint: Every library can carry a manifest.

choices.text: The Android Gradle plugin adds one to every app by default
choices.why: The plugin merges manifests; the permission in section 07 came from `androidx.core`.

choices.text: From the manifest of a library the app depends on
choices.why: Right: the build merges every library's manifest with yours, which is why the merged one is worth reading after adding a dependency.

choices.text: From `targetSdk`, which adds the permissions its version requires
choices.why: `targetSdk` becomes `<uses-sdk>`; it adds no permission.

choices.text: From the debug keystore
choices.why: A signing key has nothing to do with the manifest's contents.

prompt: A phone set to Portuguese runs the planner. `values-pt/strings.xml` has `welcome` and not `app_name`. What does the launcher show under the icon?
hint: The fallback is one string at a time.

choices.text: Nothing, because the Portuguese file is incomplete
choices.why: An incomplete translation is allowed; each missing string falls back on its own.

choices.text: The resource id, `0x7f...`
choices.why: The id is how code names the string; a phone never shows it as text.

choices.text: `Planner`, the default value
choices.why: Right: `app_name` is missing from `values-pt`, so the default value is used for that one string.

choices.text: The package name, `com.example.planner`
choices.why: The label comes from `android:label`, which names the string resource.

prompt: Colours for dark mode go in a resource folder called `values-___`.
hint: Section 07 lists it with the tablet one.

prompt: Why is the debug APK of a one-sentence app 12 MB?
hint: Look at what the dex holds and what `R8 Enabled` says.

choices.text: Debug builds embed a copy of the Android framework
choices.why: The framework is on the phone; no APK carries it.

choices.text: It holds the code of every library it depends on, and nothing removed the unused parts
choices.why: Right: R8 is off in debug, so the dex is every library whole.

choices.text: The resources of `values-pt` doubled its size
choices.why: `resources.arsc` is under half a megabyte; the dex files are the bulk.

choices.text: Debug APKs are stored uncompressed
choices.why: The zip is compressed: about 29 MB of files fit into 12 MB.

prompt: How many `classes*.dex` files did the debug APK contain?
hint: `unzip -l` listed them.

prompt: You build the planner on two laptops with no key of your own. Both debug APKs are signed. Which statement is true?
hint: Where did the key come from, and what is it for?

choices.text: They are signed with your Google account, which the SDK asked for
choices.why: No account was involved; the first build made a key on disk.

choices.text: Either one is fit to publish, since it is signed
choices.why: A debug key is never what you publish with; lesson 22 makes the real one.

choices.text: Each was signed by a `~/.android/debug.keystore` the first build created
choices.why: Right: each machine makes its own debug key with a well-known password, for development only.

choices.text: Unsigned builds are refused by `assembleDebug`, so it borrowed Google's key
choices.why: Google's key is not on your machine; the debug key is generated locally.

prompt: Which of these files belong in the planner's version control? Choose all that apply.
hint: A file that names a path on your computer stays out; so does what a build regenerates.

choices.text: `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties`
choices.why: Yes: it names the exact Gradle every clone will use.

choices.text: `local.properties`
choices.why: No: `sdk.dir` is a path on one computer.

choices.text: `gradle/libs.versions.toml`
choices.why: Yes: it is where every version is pinned.

choices.text: `app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk`
choices.why: No: a build output is regenerated by `./gradlew` from the sources.

prompt: A teammate's build fails with `Dependency 'androidx.compose.runtime:runtime-saveable-android' requires ... compile against version 37`. Their build file says 36 where this project says 37. What is the least change that fixes it?
hint: Which of the three numbers is about what the compiler knows?

choices.text: Raise `targetSdk` to 37
choices.why: `targetSdk` opts into runtime behaviour; the library's check is on `compileSdk`.

choices.text: Raise `compileSdk` to 37 and install `platforms/android-37.0`
choices.why: Right: that is exactly this project's choice, and it changes nothing on a phone.

choices.text: Raise `minSdk` to 37
choices.why: That would stop every phone below Android 37 from installing the app, and the error would remain.

choices.text: Downgrade Kotlin to match the platform
choices.why: The error names the SDK the code compiles against, not the Kotlin version.
